name: tass64
desc: Multi pass optimizing macro assembler for the 65xx series of processors
why: A multi-pass optimizing macro assembler for 65xx chips, a door into retro 6502 machine code and old-school hardware programming.

brief.what_it_is: 64tass is a command-line macro assembler for the 65xx family of processors (6502, 65C02, 65816, 65CE02, 45GS02 and others). You give it an assembly source file, usually .asm, and it produces binary output, with Hex and S-record text formats also available. It is described as a multi-pass optimizing assembler with arbitrary-precision integers, Unicode-aware source handling, a built-in linker with section support, macros, structures, unions and scopes, and assembly and label listings. The manual covers an extensive expression language, including lists, tuples, dictionaries and built-in math and binary-file functions.
brief.why_it_exists: The project positions itself as a familiar, portable tool for 6502-family development, with syntax 'familiar' to Omicron TASS and TASM. The manual says that although the reference is long, 64tass 'can be used with just basic 6502 assembly knowledge in simple ways like any other assembler', and the reference is there for advanced needs.
brief.how_it_works: You run 64tass on a source file and it makes multiple passes over the source to resolve forward references and optimize addressing modes. Addressing modes are chosen from the instruction type and the .dpage, .databank and program counter settings. The manual's Makefile examples show it feeding a cruncher such as pucrunch, so the output can be a PRG file for a real or emulated machine.

commands_seen.context: Basic invocation from the manual. The -a option is 'highly recommended if the source is Unicode or ASCII'.

Makefile recipe from the manual that builds an intermediate file from source.asm. -C enables case-sensitive symbols and -B and -i select binary and ignore-case-related output options as described in the manual's option list.
The same build step written for Windows (make.bat) in the manual.
Second step in the manual's Makefile example: a third-party cruncher compresses the 64tass output into a runnable PRG. This is not part of 64tass.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond brew install was described in the homepage text I read. The manual says the source is portable C with minimal dependencies. It is a command-line tool that takes the source filename as its minimum argument. No runtime, account or configuration step was mentioned.
brief.standout: Its feature list reads like a small language: lists and tuples that apply arithmetic element-wise, dictionaries used as enumerations, bit-string and byte-string slicing, z85 binary embedding, and a binary() function that reads files such as SID music directly into source. Its stated design goal is compatibility with the old Omicron TASS workflow, which makes it a bridge between C64-era source and modern tooling.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the evidence shows. The manual is for v1.60 r3243 and labels itself a development version. The SourceForge project page lists a 'Last Update' of 2026-10-09, shows user reviews dated 2021 to 2025 with a 5.0 average from 10 reviews, and says the project was registered in 2010. The SourceForge page also credits one maintainer, 'soci'.
brief.caveats: The manual states that this is a development version and that features or syntax may change in some non-backwards-compatible ways. The homepage text I fetched was cut off at about 40,000 characters, so I did not see the full sections on the linker, listings or output formats. Licensing is GNU GPL version 2.0, from the SourceForge page. The homepage describes it as a cross assembler, and the README-equivalent does not say whether Homebrew builds it on macOS or Linux only. I did not look at the release files.
quotes: 64tass is a command line assembler, the source can be written in any text editor.

judge.reason: A capable 65xx assembler opens a hands-on path into retro hardware, with a surprisingly language-like expression system for embedding and transforming binary data.

entry.title: 64tass
entry.tldr: A command-line macro assembler for the 6502 family that turns assembly source into binaries for C64-era machines, with an unusually rich expression language.
entry.deeper_look:
64tass reads an assembly source file for a 65xx processor (6502, 65C02, 65816, 65CE02, 45GS02 and others) and writes a binary. Hex and S-record text output are also available. It makes multiple passes over the source to resolve forward references and to pick addressing modes, which it chooses from the instruction and the `.dpage`, `.databank` and program counter settings.

It exists as a portable, modern tool whose syntax is familiar to people who used Omicron TASS and TASM. That makes it a bridge between old C64-era source and today's editors and build systems. The source can be written in any text editor, and the manual's Makefile example feeds the output to a cruncher (pucrunch, a separate tool) to produce a PRG file for a real or emulated machine.

The door it opens is writing machine code for chips from the 1970s and 80s, where every byte and every addressing mode matters. The manual is long, but it says the assembler can be used with just basic 6502 knowledge, like any other assembler. The long part is for when you want more.

That extra part reads like a small language: lists and tuples, dictionaries usable as enumerations, bit-string and byte-string slicing, and a `binary()` function that pulls files such as SID music straight into source. It also has macros, structures, unions, scopes, sections with a built-in linker, and assembly and label listings.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the command-line options, including output format and case-sensitivity switches.
Assembles src.asm as ASCII/Unicode source. The manual recommends -a for such files.
The manual's Makefile recipe: builds source.asm into an intermediate file, demo.tmp, ready for a cruncher.

entry.whats_unique: Its expression language goes far beyond a typical assembler, with element-wise list arithmetic, dictionaries, and the ability to read binary files into source. It also stays compatible with the old Omicron TASS workflow.
entry.caveats: The manual calls this a development version (v1.60 r3243) and warns that syntax may change in rare non-backwards-compatible ways.
